title: We finally ran our trading strategy on real market data. The biggest problem wasn't the signals — it was the trading costs.
author: BlackGreep
selftext:
Today we completed our first end-to-end backtest of our Regime-Adaptive Trend Pullback strategy using real historical Bybit candles.

\*\*Test setup:\*\*

\- BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, SOLUSDT

\- 1-minute candles, 7-day evaluation

\- $10,000 starting equity

\- 1% planned risk per trade, including modeled costs

\- Dynamic leverage from 5× to 20×

\- Taker fee: 0.055% per side

\- Modeled slippage: 0.02% per side

\*\*Results:\*\*

\- 31 completed trades

\- 13 TP / 18 SL

\- Gross P&L: +$506.39

\- Fees: −$1,238.56

\- Slippage: −$450.39

\- Provisional P&L: \*\*−$1,182.55 (−11.83%)\*\*

\- Maximum drawdown: 13.63%

The strategy was positive before modeled costs but significantly negative afterward.

We also discovered a serious performance problem: repeated validation of the same historical data catalog inside the execution loop.

After fixing that bottleneck, the full seven-day backtest completed in 35 seconds. The original run had been interrupted after more than 46 minutes.

The backtest is still preliminary: historical funding costs aren't included, and the exchange's historical trading constraints haven't been independently verified.

\*\*Next steps:\*\* audit all 31 trades for correct fee/slippage accounting, investigate execution costs, and test a longer period without tuning the strategy to this particular week.

I'm curious how other developers handle this:

\*\*When a strategy shows positive gross P&L but deeply negative results after fees, how do you distinguish a fundamentally unprofitable strategy from an overly conservative execution model or an accounting bug?\*\*

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: you're the SOL 5-minute fees one from earlier this month, and this is the same finding on 1-minute: 31 trades paying $1,238 in fees against $506 gross means the rule's edge per trade is about a third of one round trip. the fix isn't a cheaper fee tier, it's fewer and bigger trades. the 35-second catalog fix is the better news, because now you can run the 15-minute version of the same rule tonight and see whether the costs shrink faster than the edge does.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Good catch — yes, we're seeing the same cost sensitivity again.

The $506 gross P&L covered only about 30% of the combined $1,239 in fees and $450 in modeled slippage.

We're first auditing all 31 trades to make sure costs weren't double-counted.

I agree that testing an M15 variant is worth exploring. But it would be a separate strategy version, not a direct rerun of the M1 rules. And larger positions alone wouldn't solve percentage-based trading costs.

We'll compare trade frequency, net expectancy, and cost sensitivity across versions without fitting the rules to this one week.

And yes, removing the repeated catalog validation was a major win for the engine. That optimization makes further research much more practical.

Appreciate the detailed feedback!

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: 30% of costs is a clean way to say it: the edge per trade has to triple before fees stop deciding the result. agreed the 15-minute version is a different strategy, and that's fine, what it answers is whether the signal has any edge once trades are rare enough to afford. post the audit if the fees turn out double-counted, that changes the picture.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good that you showed the cost breakdown, since many people only post the gross number. To tell a weak strategy from an accounting bug, I'd work out two or three trades by hand and check they match the engine, then compare the cost per trade with the average gross gain per trade. If the costs are bigger than the edge even at lower fees, the strategy trades too often or too small a move. Rerun it with the costs cut in half to see how sensitive it is, and keep in mind that 31 trades in a week is a small sample. Cymetica's Backtest Labs lets you set a fee percent and hold out data for a check like this.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's a solid approach, and it's actually our next step.

We're auditing all 31 trades, including manually recalculating individual fills, fees, slippage, and final P&L to rule out double-counting.

One interesting finding: if we mechanically cut both fees and slippage by 50% while keeping the same trades, the result would still be around −$338 instead of −$1,183.

That's not a proper rerun, since our cost-inclusive position sizing would also change, but it shows how significant the problem is.

I also agree that 31 trades aren't enough to evaluate the strategy's long-term edge.

We'll finish the accounting audit first, then test cost sensitivity and longer periods without tuning the rules to this specific week.

Appreciate the thoughtful feedback!

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body:
The fee/slippage ratio is a useful first check here: 1,238.56 / 450.39 is about 2.75, matching 0.055 / 0.02. That is consistent with both charges using the same aggregate notional, but it does not establish that the notional itself is correct.



For the audit, export each fill with quantity, reference price, simulated fill price and fee. Rebuild one complete round trip independently. In particular, check whether slippage is already embedded in the fill prices used for gross P&L and then subtracted again as a separate charge. Also check that leverage is not applied a second time to an already leveraged position notional.



Once that reconciles, a fixed-trade-set cost sweep would isolate the accounting effect. A full rerun is a separate test if costs change sizing or later entries. QATS team here; commenting on the test design rather than endorsing this strategy.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Excellent points, especially the distinction between consistent cost ratios and correct position notional.
We're going to independently reconstruct a few complete round trips using reference prices, simulated fills, quantities, and entry/exit fees.
We'll specifically check whether slippage is already embedded in gross P&L and whether leverage is accidentally applied twice to position notional.
Once the accounting reconciles, we'll run a fixed-trade-set cost sensitivity analysis before considering a separate full rerun.
No strategy changes until we know the financial calculations are correct.
Thanks for the detailed technical feedback — this is exactly the kind of scrutiny we're building BlackGreep to support.

comments.author: bacbac870
comments.body: Congratulations you made it to the half way .. i faced that problem 8 months ago.. there was real edge but too small that the costs eats it's before it cummulate .. i assume you are doing high frequency trades or scalp.. you have to work on bigger price movement.. bigger chart .. let's say 1 day trades not 1 hour trades .. if you find an edge it will beat the costs

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Thanks, and I think you're pointing at the core issue here.

We’ve now completed an independent financial audit of all 31 trades, including every accounting point. No double-counted slippage, fees, or leverage errors were found.

The seven-day result was +$506 gross, but approximately $1,689 in modeled fees and slippage. So the cost problem is real within our current execution assumptions, not an accounting bug.

You're right that we need a better ratio between the price movement captured and the cost of executing the trade.

The current strategy is short-term intraday, using 1-minute data. I'm considering testing higher-timeframe variants separately, rather than changing the original strategy based on one bad week.

First, we're going to evaluate the existing version over a longer historical period and then independently validate it.

Out of curiosity, when you faced this issue, did increasing the timeframe help more than simply filtering out weaker trades?

replies.author: bacbac870
replies.body: Defining weaker trades depending on your strategy.. if you see it as fixed values that you have to reach to get better signals you are wrong.. changing the timeframe unfortunately doesn't come without a price .. a strategy that have an edge on 1 minute scalp wouldn't work on half hour candles .. they don't see the same thing.. you have to find a strategy that fits a bigger scale .. you already have a system to measure it just try a lot a be patient about it

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's a good distinction, and I agree. Moving a 1-minute strategy to M30 doesn't automatically preserve its edge. It effectively becomes a different strategy that needs its own validation.

That's also why I don't want to start adjusting RSI, volatility filters, or other thresholds just to make this particular backtest look better.

We're building BlackGreep around reproducible research, so the plan is to finish evaluating the current version first, then test higher-timeframe hypotheses separately.

The one thing I'd add is that testing lots of variations comes with an overfitting risk. That's why we're also working on independent OOS validation and tracking repeated holdout exposure.

Appreciate the advice. It's exactly the kind of problem we're trying to make easier to investigate systematically.
